name.text: Relations & Functions — is this set of ordered pairs a function?

questiontext.text:
A relation is given by the set of ordered pairs

\[ \{ ({@pairs[1][1]@}, {@pairs[1][2]@}),\ ({@pairs[2][1]@}, {@pairs[2][2]@}),\ ({@pairs[3][1]@}, {@pairs[3][2]@}) \}. \]

(a) Is this relation a function?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) If it is a function, is it one-to-one or many-to-one? Choose "Not applicable" if it is not a function.

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
A relation fails to be a function only when the same \(x\)-value is paired with two different \(y\)-values. Repeated \(y\)-values are allowed: they make the function many-to-one, not "not a function". A function is one-to-one when no \(y\)-value is repeated either.

[[if test="is(scenario=0)"]]

Here the \(x\)-value \({@p1@}\) appears twice, paired with \({@q1@}\) and with \({@q2@}\). One input has two outputs, so the relation is not a function. Part (b) is not applicable.

[[elif test="is(scenario=1)"]]

Here the \(x\)-values \({@p1@}\), \({@p2@}\) and \({@p3@}\) are all different, so each input has exactly one output and the relation is a function. The \(y\)-value \({@q1@}\) is shared by \(x = {@p1@}\) and \(x = {@p2@}\), so two inputs have the same output. The function is many-to-one.

[[else]]

Here the \(x\)-values \({@p1@}\), \({@p2@}\) and \({@p3@}\) are all different, so the relation is a function. The \(y\)-values \({@q1@}\), \({@q2@}\) and \({@q3@}\) are also all different, so no two inputs share an output. The function is one-to-one.

[[/if]]

questiondescription.text: This question is based on the definitions of one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many relations in Section 16.1 (Types of Relations) of the Grade 11 Functions topic. It targets the misconception that repeated y-values stop a relation being a function.

falsefeedback.text:
[[if test="is(scenario=1)"]]

Repeated \(y\)-values do not stop a relation from being a function. Only a repeated \(x\)-value with two different \(y\)-values does that. Check the \(x\)-values again.

[[elif test="is(scenario=0)"]]

Look for an \(x\)-value that appears in more than one pair. A relation is not a function when the same \(x\)-value is paired with two different \(y\)-values.

[[else]]

A relation fails to be a function only when the same \(x\)-value is paired with two different \(y\)-values. Check whether any \(x\)-value appears more than once.

[[/if]]

Decide part (a) first: one-to-one and many-to-one describe functions only. For a function, compare the \(y\)-values. It is many-to-one when two different \(x\)-values share a \(y\)-value, and one-to-one when every \(y\)-value appears only once.
